# Exercise 4.1 — One interface, many models {#sec-frameworks}

**45 minutes · work individually**

## Objectives

::: {.objective-list}
- Say what a model *specification* is, what an *engine* is, and which of the two
  you change to swap one algorithm for another.
- Fit three different models to the same rows by changing one line each time,
  and score each against a baseline that does no learning.
- Say what a `workflow` or a `Pipeline` carries that a fitted model on its own
  does not.
:::

## Why this, here

In @sec-pipeline you wrote the five steps out by hand, with `lm()` in R and
`LinearRegression()` in Python. That is affordable for one model. From today the
models multiply — logistic regression now, trees and forests on @sec-day5 — and
each one of them has its own function name, its own argument names and its own
way of returning a prediction. `rpart()` wants `method = "class"`;
`randomForest()` wants the outcome to be a factor and will quietly do regression
if it is not; `glmnet()` refuses a formula and demands a matrix.

Two ecosystems exist to put one interface in front of all of that: **tidymodels**
in R and **scikit-learn** in Python. The point of this exercise is not that they
save typing. It is that they make models *comparable*: when the only line that
differs between two analyses is the one naming the model, the difference in the
result is attributable to the model.

| The question | tidymodels | scikit-learn |
|---|---|---|
| what kind of model is this | `logistic_reg()`, `decision_tree()` | the estimator class, `LogisticRegression` |
| which code actually fits it | `set_engine("glm")` | the class, plus `solver=` |
| what happens to the data first | a `recipe()` of `step_*()` | transformers, e.g. `StandardScaler` |
| the two bolted together | `workflow()` | `Pipeline` |
| fit it, then use it | `fit()`, `predict()` | `.fit()`, `.predict()` |

: {tbl-colwidths="[30,35,35]"}

## A specification is not a model

Declaring a model and fitting it are separate acts, and both frameworks make you
notice. In R you can print a specification that has never seen data. In Python
the estimator exists, but asking it to predict raises an error until you fit it.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
library(tidymodels)

log_spec  <- logistic_reg(mode = "classification") |> set_engine("glm")
tree_spec <- decision_tree(mode = "classification") |> set_engine("rpart")

log_spec
```

## Python

```{python}
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.exceptions import NotFittedError

log_spec = LogisticRegression(C=float("inf"), max_iter=1000)

try:
    log_spec.predict([[120.0, 30.0, 40.0]])
except NotFittedError as e:
    print(str(e).split(".")[0])
```
:::

The R specification says *logistic regression, fitted by `glm`* and nothing else:
no data, no coefficients. Swapping `"glm"` for `"glmnet"` keeps the first half
and replaces the second.

## The split we use all day

`data/diabetes.csv` holds 768 patients: eight measurements and `diabetes`, which
is `pos` or `neg`. It is the synthetic replacement for the withdrawn Pima Indians
data — read @sec-data-diabetes before you quote a number from it anywhere.

We hold back every fifth row. That is not how you would usually split, and the
reason we do it here is worth a paragraph.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why a fixed rule rather than a seed
@sec-pipeline showed that `set.seed(42)` and `random_state=42` select different
rows, so the two languages ended the day with different test sets and different
scores. That is honest, but it means any R-versus-Python difference you then see
is confounded with the split.

Taking every fifth row of a file whose row order carries no information gives
both languages *the same 153 patients*, so the rest of this day compares
languages rather than partitions. Exercise 1.2's Stretch 2 asked how much the
split matters; Stretch 1 below is that question again, and the answer is still
"more than you would like".
:::

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
library(readr); library(dplyr)

diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))

test_rows <- seq(5, nrow(diabetes), by = 5)
train <- diabetes[-test_rows, ]
test  <- diabetes[ test_rows, ]

c(train = nrow(train), test = nrow(test), test_pos = sum(test$diabetes == "pos"))
```

## Python

```{python}
import pandas as pd

diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")

is_test = (diabetes.index + 1) % 5 == 0
train, test = diabetes[~is_test], diabetes[is_test]

y_train = (train["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)
y_test  = (test["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)
features = ["glucose", "mass", "age"]

len(train), len(test), int(y_test.sum())
```
:::

## Fit and predict: the same two verbs, whatever the model

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
log_fit  <- log_spec  |> fit(diabetes ~ glucose + mass + age, data = train)
tree_fit <- tree_spec |> fit(diabetes ~ glucose + mass + age, data = train)

acc <- function(f) mean(predict(f, test)$.pred_class == test$diabetes)
c(logistic = acc(log_fit), tree = acc(tree_fit),
  majority = mean(test$diabetes == "neg"))
```

## Python

```{python}
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

log_fit  = LogisticRegression(C=float("inf"), max_iter=1000).fit(train[features], y_train)
tree_fit = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42).fit(train[features], y_train)

{"logistic": round(log_fit.score(test[features], y_test), 4),
 "tree":     round(tree_fit.score(test[features], y_test), 4),
 "majority": round(float((y_test == 0).mean()), 4)}
```
:::

Two readings, and the second is the uncomfortable one.

The logistic regressions agree: 0.712 in both languages, on the same 153
patients. The trees do not — about 0.69 in R against about 0.59 in Python — and
the word `decision_tree` is identical in both. `rpart` stops growing when a split
stops paying for itself, so it returns ten leaves; `DecisionTreeClassifier` grows
until every leaf is pure, so it returns about 180 and scores 1.00 on the rows it
was fitted to. Same name, same data, different default, and the default is the
whole difference. @sec-decision-trees is where you learn to control it.

And a third reading, which should take the shine off all of them: always saying
`neg` scores 0.641 on this test set. The logistic model's seven percentage points
over that is the entire return on three clinical measurements.

## Task 1 — Swap the model, keep everything else

Fit a third model — a random forest, five hundred trees instead of one — on the
same rows, and score it against the majority baseline. One line names the model;
nothing else changes.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")
rf_fit <- rand_forest(mode = "classification") |>
  set_engine("ranger", seed = 42) |>
  fit(______, data = ______)

acc_rf <- mean(predict(rf_fit, test)$.pred_class == test$diabetes)
check_beats_prevalence(acc_rf, test$diabetes)
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
source("checks/checks.R")
rf_fit <- rand_forest(mode = "classification") |>
  set_engine("ranger", seed = 42) |>
  fit(diabetes ~ glucose + mass + age, data = train)

acc_rf <- mean(predict(rf_fit, test)$.pred_class == test$diabetes)
check_beats_prevalence(acc_rf, test$diabetes)
```
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

rf_fit = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42).fit(______, ______)

acc_rf = rf_fit.score(test[features], y_test)
check_beats_prevalence(acc_rf, y_test)
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier

rf_fit = RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42).fit(train[features], y_train)

acc_rf = rf_fit.score(test[features], y_test)
check_beats_prevalence(acc_rf, y_test)
```
:::
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
The R side wants the same formula and the same data frame you gave `fit()` for
the logistic model. The Python side wants the predictor columns and the outcome
as two separate arguments — that is the shape difference from Exercise 1.1, and
it has not gone away.
:::

A forest has no coefficients, no equation and no way of telling a clinician why
it said what it said. It also, here, does not win: five hundred trees score
about 0.69–0.70 against the logistic regression's 0.712 on the same rows. Note
that down before @sec-random-forest, and note too that the cost of finding it
out was one line — which is the argument for the framework, and the only
argument this exercise is making.

## Task 2 — Swap the engine, keep the model

Now change only the second half of the specification. In R, replace the `glm`
engine with `glmnet`, which fits the same logistic model with a penalty on the
coefficients. In Python there is no engine slot; the nearest thing is `solver=`,
so change that instead and see whether it does the same job.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
lasso_fit <- logistic_reg(penalty = 0.1, mixture = 1) |>
  set_engine("______") |>
  fit(diabetes ~ glucose + mass + age, data = train)

round(coef(lasso_fit$fit, s = 0.1)[, 1], 5)   # compare with the glm coefficients
round(coef(log_fit$fit), 5)
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
lasso_fit <- logistic_reg(penalty = 0.1, mixture = 1) |>
  set_engine("glmnet") |>
  fit(diabetes ~ glucose + mass + age, data = train)

round(coef(lasso_fit$fit, s = 0.1)[, 1], 5)
round(coef(log_fit$fit), 5)
```
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import numpy as np
for solver in ["lbfgs", "newton-cg", "______"]:
    m = LogisticRegression(C=1.0, solver=solver, max_iter=1000).fit(train[features], y_train)
    print(f"{solver:>10}", np.round(m.coef_[0], 5), round(m.intercept_[0], 3))
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
import numpy as np
for solver in ["lbfgs", "newton-cg", "liblinear"]:
    m = LogisticRegression(C=1.0, solver=solver, max_iter=1000).fit(train[features], y_train)
    print(f"{solver:>10}", np.round(m.coef_[0], 5), round(m.intercept_[0], 3))
```
:::
:::
:::

In R the engine change is a change of model: the lasso drives the coefficients
for `mass` and `age` to exactly zero and keeps only `glucose`. Two of your three
predictors have left the building, and nothing in the specification said they
could.

In Python two of the three solvers agree to four decimal places and the third,
`liblinear`, does not — it penalises the intercept as well, which the other two
do not. So "the solver is only a numerical detail" is true twice out of three
times, which is the worst possible number of times for a thing to be true.

## Task 3 — Put preprocessing inside the model object

A `workflow` and a `Pipeline` are the same idea: one object that remembers both
what you did to the data and what you fitted to it, so that the identical
treatment reaches the test rows. Build one with the predictors standardised.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")
rec <- recipe(diabetes ~ glucose + mass + age, data = train) |>
  step_normalize(______)

wf_fit <- workflow() |>
  add_model(log_spec) |>
  add_recipe(______) |>
  fit(data = train)

acc_wf <- mean(predict(wf_fit, test)$.pred_class == test$diabetes)
check_beats_prevalence(acc_wf, test$diabetes)
round(coef(extract_fit_engine(wf_fit)), 4)
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
source("checks/checks.R")
rec <- recipe(diabetes ~ glucose + mass + age, data = train) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

wf_fit <- workflow() |>
  add_model(log_spec) |>
  add_recipe(rec) |>
  fit(data = train)

acc_wf <- mean(predict(wf_fit, test)$.pred_class == test$diabetes)
check_beats_prevalence(acc_wf, test$diabetes)
round(coef(extract_fit_engine(wf_fit)), 4)
```
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

pipe = Pipeline([
    ("scale", ______),
    ("model", LogisticRegression(C=float("inf"), max_iter=1000)),
]).fit(train[features], y_train)

acc_pipe = pipe.score(test[features], y_test)
check_beats_prevalence(acc_pipe, y_test)
np.round(pipe[-1].coef_[0], 4), round(pipe[-1].intercept_[0], 4)
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

pipe = Pipeline([
    ("scale", StandardScaler()),
    ("model", LogisticRegression(C=float("inf"), max_iter=1000)),
]).fit(train[features], y_train)

acc_pipe = pipe.score(test[features], y_test)
check_beats_prevalence(acc_pipe, y_test)
np.round(pipe[-1].coef_[0], 4), round(pipe[-1].intercept_[0], 4)
```
:::
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Assign the result of `.fit()`, always
Written as a bare line, `pipe.fit(X, y)` returns the fitted pipeline, and both
Jupyter and this booklet will then print scikit-learn's HTML representation of
it — the grey box listing every default parameter. It is noise in a notebook,
and in a `knitr` render under a non-UTF-8 locale it stops the build outright.
Assign the result, or end the line with a semicolon.
:::

Compare the standardised coefficients with the unstandardised ones from the
earlier cell. The accuracy is unchanged at 0.712 — an unpenalised logistic
regression does not care about the units of its predictors — but the
coefficients now say something the originals could not: per standard deviation,
`glucose` carries about four times the weight of `mass` or `age`.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Two things differ between the languages here, and only one matters
R reports the standardised `glucose` coefficient as about 1.1804 and Python as
about 1.1794. The cause is that `step_normalize()` divides by the sample standard
deviation (dividing by $n-1$) and `StandardScaler` by the population one
(dividing by $n$). It is a convention, it is a fourth decimal place, and it never
changed a clinical conclusion.

The difference that *does* matter is in the next section.

The reason to put the scaling inside the object rather than before the split is
leakage: a scaler fitted on all 768 rows has read the test set's mean. That is
@sec-leakage's subject and this is the machinery that prevents it.
:::

## The result that should bother you

The two frameworks give you the same interface. They do not give you the same
model.

1. On these 615 training rows, R's `glm` and scikit-learn with `C=inf` agree to
   five decimal places: `glucose` 0.03508, `mass` 0.03598, `age` 0.02170. Whatever
   else is going on, the two libraries solve the same problem when you ask them
   to.
2. But `C=inf` is not scikit-learn's default. The default is `C=1.0`, which is an
   L2 penalty on the coefficients — the thing the `glmnet` engine does in R only
   when you ask for it. On 615 rows the penalty is swamped by the likelihood and
   you cannot see it.
3. Run the cell below, which refits on the first 50 rows only. Now you can.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
small <- diabetes[1:50, ]
z <- function(x) (x - mean(x)) / sd(x)
glm_small <- glm(diabetes ~ z(glucose) + z(mass) + z(age) + z(pedigree),
                 data = small, family = binomial)
round(coef(glm_small), 3)
```

## Python

```{python}
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import numpy as np

small = diabetes.iloc[:50]
y_small = (small["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)
f4 = ["glucose", "mass", "age", "pedigree"]

for C, label in [(float("inf"), "no penalty"), (1.0, "the default")]:
    p = Pipeline([("scale", StandardScaler()),
                  ("model", LogisticRegression(C=C, max_iter=2000))]).fit(small[f4], y_small)
    print(f"{label:>12}", dict(zip(f4, np.round(p[-1].coef_[0], 3))))
```
:::

Unpenalised, `mass` has a coefficient of −0.022; at the default `C=1.0` it is
+0.035. Fifty patients, four predictors, and the sign of a clinical
association depends on an argument nobody typed. R's unpenalised `glm` gives −0.022
too: it matches the unpenalised Python fit, not Python's default.

The lesson is not that scikit-learn is wrong — a penalty on 50 rows is good
statistics, and Day 5 will argue for it. The lesson is that **"I fitted a
logistic regression" does not identify a model**, and a methods section that says
only that cannot be reproduced in the other language.

## Reflection

1. You now have four fitted objects that all answer `predict()`. Name one thing
   a reviewer could ask about your analysis that none of them can answer, and
   say which object would have to carry it.
2. A colleague reports that their Python results do not match yours and asks for
   your R script. What is the shortest list of things they must check before
   concluding that one of you has made a mistake?

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Expected values** (the data is synthetic; the last digit may move if it is
regenerated). Test set 153 rows, 55 `pos`. Accuracy: logistic 0.71 in both
languages, `rpart` tree ≈ 0.69, scikit-learn tree ≈ 0.59, random forest ≈ 0.69–0.70,
majority baseline 0.641. Unstandardised `glm`/`C=inf` coefficients: intercept
≈ −6.94, glucose ≈ 0.0351, mass ≈ 0.0360, age ≈ 0.0217. Standardised: ≈ 1.18,
0.29, 0.26. The `glmnet` lasso at `penalty = 0.1` keeps `glucose` (≈ 0.018) and
zeroes `mass` and `age`.

**Answers.** (1) Anything about uncertainty or about which rows were used:
`predict()` returns a point prediction and none of these objects carries a
confidence interval, a record of the split, or the package version. A `workflow`
or `Pipeline` carries the preprocessing but not the provenance; that is why
registries exist (@sec-pipeline). (2) The short list: the same rows, the same
predictors, the same penalty, the same treatment of the outcome's level order.
Three of the four are invisible in a script that only says
`LogisticRegression()`.

**Common failures.** (1) `fit(diabetes ~ ., data = train)` in Task 1 — it runs,
scores better, and is not the same model; ask what `.` included. (2) In Python,
`train[features]` written as `train["glucose"]`, giving a shape error, exactly as
in Exercise 1.1. (3) a missing engine package: the specification prints happily and `fit()`
fails, which illustrates the specification/engine split well and wastes ten
minutes badly — check `ranger` and `glmnet` are installed before the session.

**Timing.** Tasks 1 and 3 are the load-bearing ones. Task 2 can be demonstrated
from the front in four minutes if the room is slow.
:::
:::

## Stretch

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 1 — How much of today is the split?
Replace the every-fifth-row rule with `initial_split(diabetes, prop = 0.8,
strata = diabetes)` under ten different seeds, and collect the ten logistic
accuracies. Ours ran from about 0.69 to 0.80. The majority baseline moves too.
Report the range, and then decide what you think of a paper that reports one
split and three decimal places.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 2 — Make the tree behave
Grow the scikit-learn tree with `ccp_alpha=0.01` and refit. The test accuracy
rises from about 0.59 to about 0.71. You have not changed the algorithm, the
data or the split — only the default that decides when to stop. Keep the number:
@sec-decision-trees is about why pruning is the whole game.
:::

## What you can and cannot now claim

**Can:** that you can fit, swap and score models through one interface in either
language, and that you know which line to change to swap the algorithm, the
engine or the preprocessing.

**Cannot:** that any of these models is any good. Every number on this page is
an accuracy, and accuracy on a 36% prevalence outcome is a weak instrument —
0.641 of it is free. Before judging a classifier you need to know what it
predicts for an individual patient, which is a probability, and that is
@sec-logistic-regression.
